full_judgment:
Nazmun Ara Sultana, J. This Civil Appeal, by leave, at the instance of Dhaka Nawab Court of Wards Estate represented by Chairman, Court of Wards and Chairman, Land Reforms Board and Dhaka Nawab Court of Wards Estate represented by Manager, Land Reforms Board has arisen out of the judgment and order dated 05.04.2003 passed by the High Court Division in First Appeal No. 229 of 2001 rejecting the prayer for withdrawal of the suit and also dismissing the appeal. These appellants, as plaintiffs, instituted Title Suit No. 15 of 1999 in the Court of Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Dhaka for declaration of title in the suit property stating, inter-alia, that the suit property originally belonged to Nawab Sir Salimullah which devolved upon the Court of Wards under the Court of Wards Act, 1879 and the land was recorded in the C.S. Khatian and also S.A. Khatian in the name of Court of Wards on behalf of Nawab Sir Salimullah. That the property cannot be given in settlement by anybody other than Board of Revenue of the Court of Wards, but the defendants claimed title over the suit property on the' basis of alleged settlements allegedly granted in their favour by the chief Manager of Court of Wards, that the alleged settlements of the suit land in favour of the defendants are fraudulent, collusive and illegal and that these alleged settlements created cloud in the title of the plaintiffs and hence the plaintiffs felt constrained to institute the suit. 

 2. The defendant Nos. 9 to 18 contested the suit by filing written statement contending, inter-alia, that the suit was not maintainable, that the Chief Manager of the Court of Wards settled the suit property in favour of the defendant Nos. 1 to 8 before the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act came into force and after getting settlement the defendant Nos. 1 to. 8 were enjoying the suit properties on payment of revenue and taxes and the suit properties also were recorded in their names. That these defendants along with 29 others purchased the suit land from the settlement holders by 32 different registered kabalas and the khatians also were prepared in their names and they paid rents and have been possessing the suit property. That in an earlier snit being Title Suit No. 386 of 1989 this present plaintiff No. 1 filed written statement admitting that the manager of the Court of Wards though did not possess the power to settle the lands situated in Dhaka City, but he had the power to do so for the lands situated outside Dhaka City. That the settlements of the suit property by the manager of the Court of Wards in favour of the vendors of the contesting defendants were valid in law. 

 8. Mr. A. F. Hasan Ariff, the learned Counsel for the plaintiff-appellants has made submissions to the effect that order XXIII rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure has authorized the court to grant permission to the plaintiff to withdraw the suit with the liberty to sue afresh at any time after its institution on the ground of formal defects and also on other sufficient grounds and that by virtue of section 107 of the same Code of Civil Procedure the appellate court also possesses this power of granting permission to the plaintiff-appellants to withdraw from the suit; that in the present case the plaintiff-appellants filed an application before the appellate court for withdrawal of the suit stating clearly that there were some formal defects for which the suit might fail, but the appellate court, without considering at all the grounds stated in that application for withdrawal of the suit, rejected the same on the ground only that the said application was filed at a belated stage. Mr. Hasan Ariff has argued that where the law permits withdrawal of the suit at any time after its institution and where it is now settled by so many decisions of the apex courts that a suit can be withdrawn at the appellate stage also, the High Court Division was not justified at all in rejecting the application for withdrawal of the suit on the ground only that it was filed at a belated stage. The learned Counsel has argued that the High Court Division ought to have considered the ground for withdrawal of the suit mentioned in that application. The learned Counsel has contended that had the High Court Division considered the grounds for withdrawal of the suit it would not have rejected the application on the plea only that it was filed at a belated stage. The learned Counsel has stated also about the formal defects of the suit. He has stated that some other persons also require to be added as defendants in this suit and prayer for some consequential reliefs, such as confirmation of possession and permanent injunction against the defendants also need to be added in this suit. The learned Counsel has submitted that the High Court Division has committed error in rejecting the prayer for withdrawal of the suit without considering at all these formal defects in framing the suit and as such the impugned judgment and order is liable to be set aside. In support of his submission the learned Counsel for the plaintiff-appellants has cited the cases of Mohammed Abdul Quddus Vs. Mohammad Mustafa Hussain, reported in 12 BLD(AD) 131, Madan Mohon Vs. Abdus Samad, reported in 32 DLR at page 176 and Dil Mohammad Vs. Jamir Hossain, reported in 58 DLR at page 88. In all these cases permission for withdrawal of the suit was granted at the appellate stage on the ground of formal defect and also on other sufficient grounds. 

 10. In reply to this submission of the learned Counsel for the defendant-respondents Mr. A. F. Hasan Ariff, the learned Counsel for the plaintiff-appellants has strongly argued to the effect that nowhere either in the plaint or in deposition of the witness the plaintiff ever admitted that they were not in possession of the suit land, that the contesting defendants also, by adducing evidence, could not prove at all that the plaintiffs were out of possession or the defendants were in possession of the suit land. Mr. Hasan Ariff has also drawn our notice to the application for withdrawal of the suit and stated that in this application also it was not stated that the plaintiffs were out of possession. The learned Counsel has stated also that in the leave granting order only this court erroneously mentioned that in the application for withdrawal of the suit it was stated that the plaintiffs being out of possession there was defect in the suit. The learned Counsel has contended that it was an error made by the court and that for this erroneous statement made by the court it cannot be said at all that the plaintiff-appellants were out possession of the suit land. Mr. Hasan Ariff has argued also that on examination of all the materials on record it will be very much evident that nowhere in the plaint, nor in the evidence, nor in the application for withdrawal of the suit there is any admission at all to the effect that the plaintiffs are out of possession of the suit land and that the contesting defendants also did not try even to prove by adducing necessary evidence that the plaintiffs are out of possession or they (defendants) are in possession of the suit land. 

 12. It appears that in this suit both the contesting parties examined only one witness each in order to prove their respective cases. From the side of the plaintiff Dhaka Nawab Court of Wards Estate, one Assistant Manager of Court of Wards, Land Reforms Board was examined as P.W. 1. This witness has deposed to the effect that Court of Wards did not settle the suit land in favour of anybody and that in S.A. Khatian No. 3 the suit land has been recorded in the name of Court of Wards. This witness has produced also a photocopy of a certified copy of S.A. Khatian No. 3-(which the court marked as exhibit-3) showing that the suit land has been recorded in the name of Dhaka Nawab Court of Wards state. The P.W. 1 has specifically denied also the defence case that the Chief Manager of the Court of Wards settled the suit land in favour of the defendants and that the defendants were possessing the suit land. During cross-examination this witness of the plaintiffs has further specifically denied the defence suggestion that the plaintiffs were not possessing the suit land. It also appears that to this P.W. 1 a suggestion was put from the side of the defendants to the effect that the S.A. and R.S. Khatians of the suit land were collusive and that after getting summons of this suit the defendants could know about these S.A. and R.S. Khatians of the suit lands. This defence suggestion, rather, supports the plaintiffs' case that 'the suit land has been recorded in the S.A. and R.S. Khatians in the name of the plaintiff. 

 13. D.W. 1, the only witness from the side of the contesting defendant, though deposed to the effect that the suit land was settled in their favour, but it appears that none of these alleged settlements of the suit land in favour of the defendants have been proved at all. This D.W. 1 though produced some alleged certified copies of some alleged filed 'parchas' of the suit land but it appears that none of these alleged field 'parchas' has been proved to be genuine. Where the defendants admitted that the suit land was recorded in the name of the Dhaka Nawab Court of Wards Estate in both 'S.A. and R.S. Khatians by giving specific suggestion to the D.W. 1 to the effect that both those khatians were collusive-the alleged field 'parchas' of the suit land should have been taken into consideration cautiously. But it appears that no attempt was mate either from the side of the defendants or from the side of the court to be sure that those alleged field 'parchas' produced by the D.W. 1 were genuine though from the side of the plaintiffs it was specifically alleged by giving suggestion to the D.W. 1 that those field 'parchas' were collusive. However, it appears that this D.W. 1, during cross-examination, has stated that he was defendant No. 16, and was deposing on his behalf only and that the other defendants did not give him any power to depose of their behalf also. To this D.W. 1 specific suggestion was given from the side of the plaintiffs that the defendants did not possess the suit land. 

 14. In this suit it is an admitted fact that the suit land belonged to the plaintiff Dhaka Nawab Court of Wards Estate and the plaintiff was also in possession of the suit land. In these circumstances, in this suit, the onus is heavily upon the contesting defendants to prove their alleged case that they took Settlement of the suit land from the Chief Manager of the plaintiff Dhaka Nawab Court of Wards Estate and they got possession of the same and are also in possession of the same. But it appears that except the D.W. 1-one of the contesting defendants himself-no other witness has been examined before the court either to prove the alleged settlement of the suit land in favour of the defendants or to prove the defendants' possession in the suit land. In these circumstances how the courts below could say that the plaintiffs had no title and possession in the suit land and also that the defendants are in possession of the suit land. It appears that the High Court Division did not at all examine the evidence on record, rather made some statements in the impugned judgment to the effect that the trial court considered the evidence adduced by the contesting defendants and found title in favour of the defendants. The High Court Division itself, in spite of being the appellate court, did not examine the evidence adduced by the parties and did not consider at all whether the findings and decisions of the trial court was justified and correct without examining the evidence on record and without forming any opinion of its own as to the truth, genuineness, acceptability etc. of the evidence adduced by the parties the High Court Division dismissed the appeal simply making comment to the effect that since the plaintiff could not prove their possession in the suit land and since the defendants had been found in possession the suit has been rightly dismissed. We don't understand how the High Court Division could say that the defendants have been found in possession of the suit land where the trial court also did not find possession of the defendants in the suit land. It appears that the High Court Division in its impugned judgment stated also that the only witness of the plaintiffs did not assert that the plaintiffs are in possession of the suit land. But on scrutiny of the evidence of P.W. 1 we find that thin. P.W. 1 has categorically denied the defence suggestion that the plaintiffs are not in possession of the suit land. We have already pointed out before that where, admittedly, the plaintiff Dhaka Nawab Court of Wards Estate was the owner in possession of the suit land the onus is heavily upon the defendants to prove that they are now in possession of the suit land. But the defendants have failed to discharge that onus. 

 15. Mr. Hasan Aniff, the learned Counsel for the plaintiff-appellants has stated also that this plaintiff No. 1 did not file any written statement in Title Suit No. 386 of 1989 stating that the Chief Manager of the Court of Wards had authority to settle the land situated outside Dhaka City. This statement of Mr. Hasan Ariff has not been controverted by the learned Counsel of the defendant-respondents.
